docs.title: HIVE
docs.text:
Hydrodynamic Identification and Validation Environment

HIVE is a Python framework for wave energy converter (WEC) hydrodynamic modelling, identification, and model benchmarking.

docs.title: What HIVE does
docs.text:
HIVE provides structured pipelines to:

  • Process CFD simulation data
  • Validate existing physics and data-based models against CFD reference data
  • Identify model parameters and data-driven surrogates from CFD reference data

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• BEM-based linear and weakly-nonlinear hydrodynamic model
  • Viscous drag identification
  • PI gain identification for PTO control
  • Multiple and various data-based model (wave-to-force-to-velocity state-space, system identification for nonlinear dynamic (SINDY), neural network)
  • model benchmarking through large metric bank

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• environment surrogate
  • A HydroSphere BEM pickle file (r5.pkl is the project default) placed under source/models/bem/ for validation and/or identification pipeline
  • A reference raw dataset folder for placed under 'data/cfd/' for handle pipeline
  • A reference handled dataset (.csv) for validation and identification pipeline placed under data/handled/
  • A model (.json) for validation and/or identification pipeline placed under source/models/

docs.title: Quick test run
docs.text:
All scripts are run as modules from inside the code/ folder. A minimal test case is provided using r5.pkl as BEM model and out_Case_65_20_120000_-430000_example as raw reference dataset. Run it with: 

# 1 — process CFD data
python -m script.run_handle_data --case example_cases.json

# 2 — validate models
python -m script.run_validate --case example_validate.json

# 3 — identify parameters
python -m script.run_identify --case example_identify.json

Outputs land in data/handled/example_cases/ (handle data), out/validated_case/example_validate/ (validate), or models/example_identify/identification/ for identification results (identify). When repeating the test run again, a user command is required, choose [1] erase and redo all. More information is available in the user manual.

Documentation
docs.text:
This documentation is based on mkdocs and is mostly a log for the code author rather than a package documentation for external users.

To update the documentation, mkdocs gh-deploy should be ran in code/doc/

docs.title: Pipeline Overview
docs.text: HIVE is built around three pipelines ran via scripts, run_handle_data, run_validate and run_identify, each driven by a JSON input file and writing outputs to a structured folder.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Script What it does Config location Output location run_handle_data Reads raw CFD time series, applies cut times and optional resampling, computes wave parameters and hydrodynamic quantities, saves one processed dataset per case inputs/handle_case/<name>.json data/handled/<name>/ run_validate Loads processed datasets and a model.json, runs forward simulations via SimRun, computes metrics against the CFD reference, produces scatter plots over the \((H_s, T_e)\) parameter space inputs/validate_case/<name>.json out/validated_case/<name>/ run_identify Uses a scheme module (viscous_drag, pi_gain, or linear_si) to identify model parameters from CFD data, updates model.json with the result inputs/identify_case/<name>.json models/<name>/ + models/<name>/identification/

Each script read the input .json file --case <name>.json argument. The stem of that filename becomes the output folder name — choose stems that are short, lowercase, and use underscores (e.g. r5_reg).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Every plot is saved as both .png (for quick viewing) and .pkl (interactive Matplotlib figure). Reload a .pkl interactively with option [3] at the rerun prompt, or directly:

import pickle, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = pickle.load(open("plots/sea_state.pkl", "rb"))
plt.show()

docs.title: run_handle_data
docs.text: Processes raw CFD time series into a standardised format ready for validation and identification.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
python -m script.run_handle_data --case <name>.json

Config files ´.json´ live in inputs/handle_case/. The filename stem becomes the output folder name under data/handled/.

docs.title: rerun options
docs.text:
When the output folder already exists, the script prompts:

[1] erase and redo all     — reprocess + replot from scratch
[2] stop, do nothing
[3] load saved figures     — reopen existing .pkl plots interactively
[4] remake figures only    — reuse processed CSVs, regenerate plots

Option [4] is useful when tuning plot parameters without reprocessing data.

docs.title: what it does
docs.text:
1. Reads each CFD case folder from data/cfd/
  2. Instantiates a DataHandle object per case
  3. Calls processData() — computes radiation force, hydrostatic force, linear excitation force (fe_lin), and absorbed power
  4. Optionally resamples to a target dt
  5. Saves processed data and wave parameters to data/handled/<name>/data/
  6. Generates and saves plots to data/handled/<name>/plots/

docs.title: Input JSON config
docs.text:
{
  "wave_type": "regular",
  "cut_time": [50, 0],
  "duration": null,
  "hydro_sphere_pkl": "r5",
  "dt": 0.05,
  "cases": [
    {
      "T": 8.0,
      "H": 2.0,
      "damping": 120000,
      "stiffness": -280000,
      "tag": "example",
      "plot": true
    }
  ],
  "plot_options": {
    "sea_state": true,
    "power": true,
    "dynamics": true,
    "hydro": false,
    "3d": false,
    "variable": ["fe_lin", "x"]
  }
}

docs.title: top-level fields
docs.text: Field Type Description wave_type "regular" | "irregular" Type of wave used in the CFD simulation cut_time [float, float] Seconds to discard from [start, end] of the raw signal. Use 0 to keep to the edge duration float | null Maximum duration (s) to retain after the start cut. null keeps all remaining data hydro_sphere_pkl string Stem of the BEM .pkl file in source/models/bem/. e.g. "r5" loads r5.pkl dt float | null Target resampling timestep (s). null keeps the original CFD timestep cases list List of CFD cases to process (see below) plot_options dict Controls which plots are generated (see below)

docs.title: cases fields
docs.text:
Each entry in cases corresponds to one CFD run.

Field Type Required Description T float ✓ Wave period (s) — must match the CFD folder name H float ✓ Wave height (m) — must match the CFD folder name damping int ✓ PTO damping coefficient (N·s/m) stiffness int ✓ PTO stiffness coefficient (N/m), negative values allowed tag string — Optional suffix to distinguish runs with identical parameters. Appended to the case label and output filenames plot bool — Include this case in plots (default: true)

docs.title: plot_options fields
docs.text: Field Type Description sea_state bool Wave spectrum, elevation time series, and sea state grid power bool Absorbed power time series, power grid, and accumulated energy dynamics bool Displacement, velocity time series, and phase plot (x vs ẋ) hydro bool Hydrodynamic force breakdown: draft, linear forces, CFD forces, linear vs nonlinear comparisons 3d bool 3D scatter of displacement, velocity, and wave elevation variable list of strings | false One time-series plot per named column from _data.csv. e.g. ["fe_lin", "x"]

docs.title: case labels
docs.text:
Each CFD case is assigned a label derived from its parameters. The label is used as the CSV filename stem and as the series label in plots:

Hs{H}p{dec}_Te{T}p{dec}_d{damping}_k{stiffness}

Example: Hs2p0_Te8p0_d120000_k-280000

An optional "tag" field in the case config appends a suffix: Hs2p0_Te8p0_d120000_k-280000_example.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
data/handled/<name>/
├── <name>.json               ← copy of the config used
├── run.log
├── data/
│   ├── <label>_data.csv      ← full time series per CFD case
│   └── <label>_wave.csv      ← scalar wave parameters (Hs, Te, J, …)
└── plots/
    ├── <label>_sea_state.png / .pkl
    ├── <label>_power.png / .pkl
    ├── <label>_dynamics.png / .pkl
    ├── <label>_hydro.png / .pkl
    └── <label>_<variable>.png / .pkl

docs.title: time-series (_data.csv)
docs.text: Column Units Description t s Time x m Displacement xdot m/s Velocity eta m Wave elevation fe_lin N Linear excitation force (BEM convolution) fr N Radiation force fhs_lin N Linear hydrostatic force fpto N Total PTO force fd_pto N PTO damping component fs_pto N PTO spring component Pabs W Instantaneous absorbed power Pd W Damping power component Ps W Spring power component

docs.title: wave parameters (_wave.csv)
docs.text: Column Description Hs Significant wave height [m] Te Energy period [s] J Wave energy flux [W/m] eps Wave steepness

docs.title: run_identify
docs.text: Identifies model parameters or data-driven surrogates from CFD reference data using a pluggable scheme system.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
python -m script.run_identify --case <name>.json

Config files <name>.json live in inputs/identify_case/. The filename stem becomes the output folder name under source/models/.

docs.title: Rerun options
docs.text:
When the output folder already exists, the script prompts:

[1] erase and redo
[2] stop, do nothing
[3] load saved figures     — reopen existing .pkl plots interactively
[4] save with date suffix  — run and save under <name>_YYYYMMDD (keeps existing folder)

Option [4] is useful to keep previous identification results while running a new one.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Loads the base model definition from source/models/<base_model>/model.json
  2. Creates a DDFeed — loads training data and runs scheme.prep()
  3. Creates an Optimizer — owns simulation helpers and delegates to scheme.run()
  4. Computes time margins (t_warmup, t_causal) from the base model and BEM data
  5. Saves identified parameters, result JSON, simulation CSVs and plots to source/models/<name>/identification/

docs.title: Input JSON config
docs.text: The config format differs between schemes because waves_train has a different structure. Two examples are provided below.

docs.title: Example — viscous_drag
docs.text:
{
  "scheme": "viscous_drag",
  "base_model": "linear",
  "waves_train": ["example_cases"],
  "scheme_params": {
    "type": "force",
    "search": "opt",
    "c_v_min": 0,
    "c_v_max": 5000,
    "n_points": 50,
    "objective": "rmse_x"
  },
  "solver": {
    "method": "rk4",
    "dt": 0.05,
    "interpolation": {}
  }
}

docs.title: Example — pi_gain
docs.text:
{
  "scheme": "pi_gain",
  "base_model": "linear",
  "waves_train": [
    {"type": "cfd_case", "case_name": "example_cases"},
    {"type": "synthetic", "T": 7.0, "H": 2.0, "duration": 120.0}
  ],
  "scheme_params": {
    "method": "grid",
    "B_min": 0,
    "B_max": 1000000,
    "K_min": -1000000,
    "K_max": 1000000,
    "n_B": 20,
    "n_K": 20,
    "objective": {"name": "mean_P_abs", "direction": "maximize"},
    "stability": {"enabled": true, "r": 5.0},
    "n_jobs": -1
  },
  "solver": {
    "method": "rk4",
    "dt": 0.05,
    "interpolation": {}
  }
}

docs.title: Top-level fields
docs.text: Field Type Description scheme string Identification scheme to use. See Available schemes base_model string Folder name under source/models/ for the base physics model (e.g. "linear"). Must contain model.json. Use "none" to disable physics simulation waves_train list Training data sources. Format depends on scheme — see per-scheme tables below scheme_params dict Scheme-specific parameters — see per-scheme tables below solver dict Solver settings used for forward simulations during identification

docs.title: solver fields
docs.text: Field Type Description method string Integration method: "euler" | "rk2" | "rk4" (case-insensitive) dt float Simulation timestep (s) interpolation dict Per-force-term interpolation flags: {"fe": bool, "fk": bool, "eta_hs": bool}

docs.title: Multiple waves_train entries — data pooling
docs.text:
All entries in waves_train are loaded and merged into a single flat pool of wave cases. Identification runs on all of them together — there is no separate pass per entry.

For viscous_drag, this means the global \(c_v\) is optimised over the concatenated signal from all cases at once, and each case also gets its own per-case \(c_v\). Adding more entries simply widens the training distribution.

For pi_gain, gains are always per sea state — each loaded wave case gets its own optimal \((B_{pto}, K_{pto})\) regardless of how many waves_train entries there are.

docs.title: Multiple methods — method comparison
docs.text:
Both schemes accept multiple methods simultaneously (a list for pi_gain; lists for type and/or search in viscous_drag). All combinations run in the same execution. result.json stores one block per method so results can be compared.

For viscous_drag, model.json is automatically written using the method with the best global metric across all methods run. All other method results remain in result.json for manual inspection.

// viscous_drag — run all four type × search combinations in one go
"type":   ["force", "response"],
"search": ["opt", "grid"]
// → runs: force_opt, force_grid, response_opt, response_grid

// pi_gain — compare analytical, grid, and optimiser
"method": ["analytical", "opt", "grid"]

docs.title: Available schemes
docs.text:
scheme What it identifies viscous_drag Quadratic drag coefficient \(c_v\) pi_gain Per-sea-state PI controller gains \(B_{pto}\), \(K_{pto}\)

Note: linear_si is not yet implemented.

docs.title: waves_train format
docs.text:
A list of strings — each string is the stem of a handled data folder under data/handled/.

"waves_train": ["example_cases", "other_cases"]

docs.title: scheme_params fields
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description type string — Identification type: "force" (match \(f_{hyd}\)) or "response" (match \(x\), \(\dot{x}\)) search string — Search method: "opt" (scalar optimiser) or "grid" (uniform sweep) base_force string "fhyd_lin" Reference force column used when type = "force" c_v_min float — Lower bound for \(c_v\) search [N·s²/m²] c_v_max float — Upper bound for \(c_v\) search [N·s²/m²] n_points int — Number of grid points (used when search = "grid") objective string or dict "rmse_x" Objective metric. See Objectives

The four method combinations (type × search) are: force_opt, force_grid, response_opt, response_grid.

docs.title: Per-case vs global identification
docs.text:
For every method, viscous_drag always produces two \(c_v\) values:

  • per-case — \(c_v\) fitted independently to each wave case (captures sea-state variability)
  • global — single \(c_v\) fitted across all cases pooled together (what goes into model.json)

The global value is what is saved into model.json as the identified coefficient.

docs.title: Outputs — result.json
docs.text:
{
  "scheme": "viscous_drag",
  "objective": {"name": "rmse_x", "direction": "minimize"},
  "results": {
    "force_opt": {
      "c_v_global": 1850.0,
      "metric_global": 0.09,
      "metric_label": "rmse_x",
      "c_v_per_case": {"case_label_1": 1700.0, "case_label_2": 1950.0},
      "metric_per_case": {"case_label_1": 0.07, "case_label_2": 0.11},
      "c_v_mean": 1825.0,
      "c_v_std": 125.0
    }
  }
}

docs.title: waves_train format
docs.text:
A list of dicts. Each entry specifies a wave source:

"waves_train": [
  {"type": "cfd_case", "case_name": "example_cases"},
  {"type": "synthetic", "T": 7.0, "H": 2.0, "duration": 120.0}
]

cfd_case entry fields:

Field Type Description type string "cfd_case" case_name string Stem of a handled folder under data/handled/

synthetic entry fields:

Field Type Default Description type string — "synthetic" T float 7.0 Wave period (s) H float 2.0 Wave height (m) duration float 120.0 Signal duration (s) d float 200.0 Water depth (m)

Note: pi_gain uses SELF_LOADING = True — it does not call load_training_data and handles wave loading internally.

docs.title: scheme_params fields
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description method string or list "opt" Method(s) to run: "analytical" | "opt" | "grid". Accepts a list to run several methods and compare B_min float 0.0 Lower bound for \(B_{pto}\) [N·s/m] B_max float 1e6 Upper bound for \(B_{pto}\) [N·s/m] K_min float -1e6 Lower bound for \(K_{pto}\) [N/m] K_max float 1e6 Upper bound for \(K_{pto}\) [N/m] n_B int 20 Grid points along \(B\) axis (used when method = "grid") n_K int 20 Grid points along \(K\) axis (used when method = "grid") B_init float midpoint of range Initial value for "opt" K_init float midpoint of range Initial value for "opt" objective string or dict {"name": "mean_P_abs", "direction": "maximize"} Objective metric. See Objectives stability dict {"enabled": false, "r": 5.0} Early-stop stability check: stops integration if \|x − η\| > r. r defaults to the buoy radius if available n_jobs int 1 Parallel workers for grid search (-1 = all CPU cores)

method = "analytical" requires that handled cases carry wave parameters (Te). It uses BEM data to compute complex-conjugate control gains directly — no simulation loop needed for identification.

docs.title: Outputs — result.json
docs.text:
{
  "scheme": "pi_gain",
  "base_model": "linear",
  "objective": {"name": "mean_P_abs", "direction": "maximize"},
  "stability": {"enabled": true, "r": 5.0},
  "n_cases": 12,
  "results": {
    "grid": {
      "B_per_case": {"case_label": 42000.0},
      "K_per_case": {"case_label": -15000.0},
      "metric_per_case": {"case_label": 1250.3},
      "metric_label": "mean P_abs [W]"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The objective field accepts either a string shorthand or a dict with explicit direction.

"objective": "rmse_x"

"objective": {"name": "mean_P_abs", "direction": "maximize"}
Name Description Default direction "rmse_x" RMSE of displacement \(x\) minimize "rmse_xdot" RMSE of velocity \(\dot{x}\) minimize "nrmse_x" Normalised RMSE of \(x\) minimize "nrmse_xdot" Normalised RMSE of \(\dot{x}\) minimize "mean_P_abs" Mean absorbed power \(P_{abs}\) maximize "rmse_P_abs" RMSE of absorbed power minimize

docs.title: Available base models
docs.text:
The base_model field is a folder name under source/models/. The folder must contain a model.json. BEM data (HydroSphere pickle) is loaded from source/models/bem/ as referenced inside model.json.

Folder Description linear Linear potential-flow model with state-space radiation

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
source/models/<name>/
├── <name>.json               ← copy of the config used
├── model.json                ← model definition updated with identified parameters
├── run.log
└── identification/
    ├── result.json           ← identified parameters and objective value per method
    ├── data/
    │   └── *.csv             ← simulated time series at best parameter values
    └── plots/
        ├── *.png
        └── *.pkl             ← interactive figure snapshots

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The base model must exist at source/models/<base_model>/model.json before running run_identify.
  • t_warmup and t_causal are computed automatically from the base model IRF lengths and applied as simulation clip margins to all simulated trajectories.
  • For viscous_drag, multiple waves_train entries are pooled into one training set. The global \(c_v\) (fit across all pooled cases) is written to model.json; per-case values are in result.json for inspection.
  • For pi_gain, gains are identified per sea state — there is no global coefficient. Multiple waves_train entries simply extend the set of sea states covered.
  • Running several methods at once produces one result block per method in result.json. For viscous_drag, model.json is automatically written from the best-performing method (lowest global metric). For pi_gain there is no automatic model.json — all results are in result.json.

docs.title: Solver config
docs.text:
Each entry in solvers has the following fields:

Field Type Description method string "RK4", "RK2", or "euler" dt float Integration timestep [s] interpolation dict Per-force-term interpolation flags (see below)

docs.title: interpolation
docs.text:
The precomputed force signals (\(f_e^{lin}\), nonlinear FK force, wave elevation) are evaluated on the handled data grid. During ODE integration, sub-stage evaluations may fall between grid points. The interpolation dict controls, for each force term, whether it is re-evaluated at every RK sub-stage or frozen to the value at the start of the step (zero-order hold).

The underlying grid interpolation is always piecewise linear.

Key Force term Effect when true "fe" Linear excitation force \(f_e^{lin}\) Evaluated at each RK sub-stage "fk" Nonlinear Froude–Krylov force Evaluated at each RK sub-stage "eta_hs" Wave elevation for nonlinear hydrostatic Evaluated at each RK sub-stage

Setting a key to false freezes that term within each timestep (ZOH), which is cheaper but reduces effective accuracy for that term. An empty dict {} enables interpolation for all terms and is recommended for RK4 and RK2.

"interpolation": {}                        // all terms interpolated (default)
"interpolation": {"fe": false}             // freeze excitation force, interpolate rest
"interpolation": {"fe": false, "fk": false} // freeze both, interpolate eta_hs only
Field Type Description scheme string Identification scheme: "viscous_drag", "pi_gain", or "linear_si" base_model string Folder name under models/ for the base physics model. Use "none" for linear_si. waves_train list[str] Handle config stems to use as training data scheme_params dict Scheme-specific parameters (see below) solver dict Solver configuration — same fields as validate config (see above)

docs.title: viscous_drag scheme params
docs.text: Field Description c_v_range [min, max] search range for \(c_v\) [N s²/m²] n_points Number of grid points objective Objective name (default "nrmse_x")

docs.title: pi_gain scheme params
docs.text: Field Description Kp_range [min, max] for proportional gain Ki_range [min, max] for integral gain n_points Grid resolution per dimension

docs.title: linear_si scheme params
docs.text: Field Description signal_file Path to signal CSV (relative to code/) input_signals List of input column names output_signals List of output column names identification "frequency" (VF) or "time" (N4SID) w_start, w_end Frequency range for fitting [rad/s] order_list List of VF pole orders to sweep tau_min, tau_max, n_tau Causality delay sweep parameters smooth_window ETFE smoothing window length num_block_rows N4SID block rows (Hankel matrix size)

docs.title: Validate config
docs.text:
Path: inputs/validate_case/<name>.json

{
  "models": [
    {"name": "linear"},
    {"name": "linear_viscous"}
  ],
  "wave_sources": [
    {"type": "cfd_case", "case_name": "example"}
  ],
  "solvers": [
    {"method": "RK4", "dt": 0.05, "interpolation": {}}
  ],
  "eta_inputs": [
    {"type": "true"}
  ],
  "simulation": [
    {"type": "closed_loop"}
  ],
  "plot_options": {
    "states": true,
    "forces": false
  }
}
Field Type Description models list[str] Model folder names under models/ solver.method string "RK4", "RK2", or "euler" solver.dt float Integration timestep [s] solver.interpolation dict Interpolation scheme for forcing signals (see below)

docs.title: solver.interpolation
docs.text:
The excitation force \(f_e^{lin}\) and wave elevation are precomputed on the handled data grid. At each ODE stage the solver evaluates them at intermediate time points via interpolation. The interpolation dict is passed to scipy.interpolate.interp1d:

"interpolation": {}               // default — linear interpolation
"interpolation": {"kind": "linear"}   // same as above, explicit
"interpolation": {"kind": "nearest"}  // zero-order hold (step function)
"interpolation": {"kind": "cubic"}    // cubic spline, smoothest
kind value Behaviour "linear" Piecewise linear (default, recommended) "nearest" Zero-order hold — holds value at nearest grid point "quadratic" Quadratic spline "cubic" Cubic spline — smoothest, highest cost

Using "nearest" with RK4 reduces the effective accuracy of the forcing term to first order. "linear" is a good default for all solver methods. See Models & Solvers — Forcing signal interpolation for a full discussion.

docs.title: run_validate
docs.text:
Output root: models/<model_name>/validation/

models/<model_name>/validation/
├── result.json               ← metric summary for all models and sea states
├── run.log
├── data/
│   └── <label>_simrun.csv    ← simulated time series per case per model
└── plots/
    ├── scatter_<metric>.png / .pkl
    └── timeseries_<label>.png / .pkl

docs.title: result.json structure
docs.text:
{
  "t_warmup": 15.0,
  "t_causal": 3.2,
  "models": {
    "linear": {
      "T8_H2": { "nrmse_x": 0.12, "mean_P_abs": 430.5 },
      "T10_H3": { ... }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Metric names
docs.text:
Metrics passed in the metrics list of validate and identify configs follow this pattern:

Name Description nrmse_x NRMSE on displacement nrmse_xdot NRMSE on velocity rmse_x RMSE on displacement [m] rmse_xdot RMSE on velocity [m/s] mean_P_abs Mean absorbed power [W]

See Metrics for definitions.

docs.title: Model types
docs.text:
A model in HIVE is a folder under models/ containing a model.json file. The JSON records the model's physics components, identified parameters, and metadata. Currently supported model types:

Model key Description linear Cummins equation with radiation state-space, linear PTO linear_viscous As linear, plus quadratic drag $c_v

Models identified by run_identify inherit a base model's model.json and add or update the identified parameters.

docs.title: model.json structure
docs.text:
{
  "type": "linear_viscous",
  "hydro_sphere_pkl": "r5",
  "radiation": {
    "A": [[...], ...],
    "B": [[...]],
    "C": [[...]],
    "D": [[...]]
  },
  "hydrostatic": {
    "K_hs": 142000.0
  },
  "added_mass_inf": 450.0,
  "mass": 1200.0,
  "c_v": 1850.0,
  "t_warmup": 15.0,
  "t_causal": 3.2
}

The radiation block holds the state-space matrices \((A_{rad}, B_{rad}, C_{rad}, D_{rad})\) fitted from the BEM IRF. These are written by run_handle_data during the first call that initialises the BEM data.

docs.title: SimRun
docs.text:
SimRun is the class responsible for running a single forward simulation. It:

  1. Loads the model definition from model.json
  2. Instantiates the radiation state integrator
  3. Steps the ODE forward using the chosen solver
  4. Returns a dataset attribute (a pandas.DataFrame) with the same column schema as DataHandle

Because SimRun and DataHandle expose the same .dataset and .label interface, they can be mixed in plotter calls.

docs.title: ODE solvers
docs.text:
The solver block in validate and identify configs selects the numerical integrator:

"solver": {
  "method": "RK4",
  "dt": 0.05,
  "interpolation": {}
}
Method Description RK4 4th-order Runge–Kutta (recommended) RK2 2nd-order Runge–Kutta (Heun's method) euler Forward Euler (1st order, fast but inaccurate)

The integration timestep dt is independent of the CFD data's native timestep. HIVE interpolates the forcing signals (wave elevation, excitation force) onto the solver grid using the scheme specified in interpolation.

docs.title: Warmup period
docs.text:
The radiation state-space system starts at rest (\(\mathbf{z}_{rad} = 0\)). It takes several wave periods for the radiation states to converge to their quasi-steady values. HIVE computes t_warmup automatically from the pole magnitudes of \(A_{rad}\):

\[ t_{warmup} = \frac{-\log(\epsilon)}{\min_k |\text{Re}(p_k)|} \]

where \(\epsilon\) is a small tolerance (default \(10^{-3}\)) and \(p_k\) are the eigenvalues of \(A_{rad}\). The value is logged in run.log and saved in result.json.

Metrics are computed only over \([t_{warmup},\; T_{end} - t_{causal}]\).

docs.title: Why interpolation is needed
docs.text:
The excitation force \(f_e^{lin}\) and wave elevation \(\eta\) are precomputed on a fixed grid — the timestep of the handled CFD data (set by dt in the handle config). The ODE solver may use a different timestep. At each stage of the integrator (e.g. the four stages of RK4), the forcing signals must be evaluated at intermediate time points that generally do not fall on the original grid, requiring interpolation.

Note that \(f_e^{lin}\) is state-independent — it does not depend on \(x\) or \(\dot{x}\) — so it is fully precomputed before integration begins. This is unlike the radiation force \(f_{rad}\), which is stepped forward as a state-space system at each stage, or \(f_{hs}\) and \(f_{pto}\), which are evaluated from the current state.

docs.title: Interpolation schemes
docs.text:
The interpolation dict in the solver config is passed directly to scipy.interpolate.interp1d via the kind keyword:

kind Description Accuracy "linear" (default) Piecewise linear between grid points 2nd order in grid spacing "nearest" Zero-order hold — value at nearest grid point 1st order (step function) "quadratic" Piecewise quadratic spline 3rd order "cubic" Piecewise cubic spline 4th order

docs.title: Consistency with the ODE solver
docs.text:
A subtle point: if you use RK4 ("method": "RK4") but hold the forcing constant within a step ("kind": "nearest"), the integration is effectively first-order in the forcing term. The radiation and restoring forces benefit from the full RK4 accuracy, but the excitation forcing does not. For best results, match the interpolation order to the solver:

  • RK4 / RK2: use "linear" or "cubic"
  • Euler: "nearest" (ZOH) is sufficient and cheapest

In practice, "linear" is a good default — it is cheap and ensures that \(f_e^{lin}\) varies smoothly across RK stages.

docs.title: Practical note on grid resolution
docs.text: The interpolation error decreases as the handled data timestep decreases. If you notice artefacts in simulated time series (especially at high frequencies), try reducing dt in the handle config to produce a finer forcing grid, rather than switching to a higher-order interpolation scheme.
